argentinonectes:study:1.title: New plesiosaur from the uppermost Cretaceous of Patagonia sheds light on thoracic and caudal anatomy in plesiosaurs (Cretaceous Research, 2026)

facts.statement: The type locality of Argentinonectes is the Calafate Formation in Argentina.
Argentinonectes lived during the Late Cretaceous Maastrichtian age.
Argentinonectes calafatensis is known from a partial articulated skeleton discovered in 2009 under 50 cm of water in Lake Argentino, Argentina.
facts.quote: discovered in 2009. This specimen was found under 50 cm of water in Lake Argentino

facts.statement: Fernando Novas led the excavation and study of Argentinonectes, with the specimen now housed as MPM-PV 10.004 in the Padre Manuel Jesús Molina Provincial Regional Museum.
facts.quote: The specimen is now housed in the vertebrate paleontology collection of the Padre Manuel Jesús Molina Provincial Regional Museum in Santa Cruz, where it is accessioned as specimen MPM-PV 10.004

facts.statement: Initial length estimates for Argentinonectes range from 7 to 9 m, with a forelimb about 1.8 m long and hindlimbs about 1.3 m long.
facts.quote: initial estimates of its body length placed at around 7 - 9 m. The preserved forelimb is about 1.8 m long, while the hindlimbs are slightly shorter, at 1.3 m

facts.statement: Fusion of dorsal and caudal vertebrae, fused coracoids, and fully ossified limb proximities indicate the holotype was a fully grown adult.
facts.quote: These are indicators of osteological maturity, meaning the holotype individual was fully grown when it died.

facts.statement: Its dorsal vertebrae have T‑shaped transverse processes, and the humerus shows a strong sigmoid curvature with an expanded inner base for ulna articulation.
facts.quote: T-shaped cross-sections of the transverse processes on the dorsal vertebrae, an expansion on the inner surface of the base of the humerus for articulation with the ulna, a humerus with strong sigmoid curvature

facts.statement: The phalanges of Argentinonectes are spool‑like with polygonal articular facets.
facts.quote: phalanges with a spool-like morphology that have expanded articular facets with a polygonal shape

facts.statement: Costal ribs likely moved transversely for respiration, allowing breathing and swimming to occur simultaneously.
facts.quote: costal ribs likely moved transversely for respiration, entirely decoupled from the movement of the flippers

facts.statement: The ribs and gastralia are pachyostotic, a condition that helps marine tetrapods maintain buoyancy.
facts.quote: ribs and gastralia are pachyostotic (thickened with extra bone layers), a feature common in marine tetrapods that helps to maintain buoyancy

facts.statement: Phylogenetic analyses place Argentinonectes within the elasmosaurid clade Weddellonectia, often as the sister taxon to Chubutinectes.
facts.quote: all iterations recovered it within the elasmosaurid plesiosaur clade Weddellonectia. Most versions placed it as the sister taxon to Chubutinectes

facts.statement: Parallel scratches on the coracoid of Argentinonectes were probably produced by scavenging sharks shedding teeth.
facts.quote: Parallel scratches observed on the surface of the coracoid of Argentinonectes were likely made by these sharks, which shed some of their teeth as they scavenged the carcass.

facts.statement: Shark teeth of Protosqualus argentinensis, Notidanodon (or Xampylodon) dentatus, and Echinorhinus maremagnum were found near the holotype of Argentinonectes.
facts.quote: Several isolated shark teeth were found in close association to the holotype of A. calafatensis. These could be assigned to the species Protosqualus argentinensis (a dogfish shark), Notidanodon (or Xampylodon) dentatus (a cow shark), and Echinorhinus maremagnum (an extinct species of Echinorhinus).

facts.statement: The genus Argentinonectes was named by Novas et al. in 2026.
facts.quote: PBDB name: Argentinonectes (genus), Novas et al. 2026

facts.statement: Argentinonectes belongs to the family Elasmosauridae within the parent group Weddellonectia.
Argentinonectes is classified as a reptile.
Argentinonectes lived during the Maastrichtian, from about 72.2 to 66 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Maastrichtian to Maastrichtian (72.2 to 66 million years ago)

facts.statement: Only one fossil occurrence of Argentinonectes has been recorded.
